PHYSICIAN ORDERS FOR LIFE-SUSTAINING TREATMENT (POLST) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Lee

ABOUT THIS PHYSICIAN ORDERS FOR LIFE-SUSTAINING TREATMENT (POLST) FORM
This document concerns a Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment (POLST) form for Jordan Alex Lee, prepared under Part 4 (commencing with Section 4780) of Division 4.7 of the California Probate Code. A POLST form is a category of "request regarding resuscitative measures" under that Part. It is a set of medical orders — not an advance health care directive — completed by a health care provider and signed by both Jordan Alex Lee (or Jordan Alex Lee's legally recognized health care decisionmaker, Morgan Lee) and a physician, or a nurse practitioner or physician assistant acting under a physician's supervision. This document states facts about what California's Probate Code says a POLST form is and how it operates; it does not recommend whether Jordan Alex Lee should complete one, what medical treatments to choose, or how to fill out its clinical order sections. A POLST form itself, as approved by the Emergency Medical Services Authority, is a separate clinical form completed with a health care provider — this document does not replace it.

WHAT THE STATUTE DEFINES A POLST FORM TO BE
Under the Probate Code, a “request regarding resuscitative measures” is defined as a written document, signed by (A) an individual with capacity, or a legally recognized health care decisionmaker, and (B) the individual’s physician, that directs a health care provider regarding resuscitative measures. That defined category includes both a prehospital “do not resuscitate” form and a Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment (POLST) form approved by the Emergency Medical Services Authority. The statute separately defines a “Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form” as a request regarding resuscitative measures that directs a health care provider regarding resuscitative and life-sustaining measures — meaning a POLST form is the broader category's version that covers life-sustaining measures generally, not only resuscitation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Request regarding resuscitative measures” means a written document, signed by (A) an individual with capacity, or a legally recognized health care decisionmaker, and (B) the individual’s physician, that directs a health care provider regarding resuscitative measures. A request regarding resuscitative measures is not an advance health care directive."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), definition of “request regarding resuscitative measures” and that it is not an advance health care directive (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4780.)
  "(A) A prehospital “do not resuscitate” form as developed by the Emergency Medical Services Authority or other substantially similar form. (B) A Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form, as approved by the Emergency Medical Services Authority."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(a)(2)-(3) (California Legislative Information text), the POLST form as one form of request regarding resuscitative measures, and its separate definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4780.)
  Known gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4780(a)), not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this specific definitional structure. This clause states only what the statute defines the form to be — it does not describe the separate EMSA-approved clinical form itself, which is not part of the codified text.

THE STATUTE'S OWN DISTINCTION BETWEEN A POLST FORM AND AN ADVANCE HEALTH CARE DIRECTIVE
The Probate Code states directly, in the same sentence that defines the category, that “a request regarding resuscitative measures is not an advance health care directive” — and a POLST form is one form of request regarding resuscitative measures. The statute also directs that, while a health care provider completes the POLST form, the provider “should inform the patient about the difference between an advance health care directive and the Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form.” Beyond stating that a POLST is not an advance health care directive and that the difference should be explained, the codified text of this Part does not itself spell out every legal distinction between the two documents (for example, it does not codify a general rule for which document controls if their terms diverge).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A request regarding resuscitative measures is not an advance health care directive."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), a request regarding resuscitative measures (which includes a POLST form) is not an advance health care directive (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4780.)
  "The health care provider, during the process of completing the Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form, should inform the patient about the difference between an advance health care directive and the Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(c) (California Legislative Information text), the provider's duty to explain the difference between the two documents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4780.)
  Known gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section (§ 4780, subdivisions (a) and (c)), not independently authored sources. The statute's own text supports that a POLST is legally distinct from an advance directive and that providers should explain the difference, but beyond those two textual points, further characterization of exactly how the two differ in legal effect is a matter of general medical/legal practice guidance, not codified statutory text, and is not asserted here as codified law.

WHO MUST SIGN A POLST FORM, AND WHO MAY EXECUTE IT ON A PATIENT'S BEHALF
By statute, a legally recognized health care decisionmaker — such as Morgan Lee, if acting in that role for Jordan Alex Lee — may execute a POLST form only if Jordan Alex Lee lacks capacity, or Jordan Alex Lee has designated that the decisionmaker's authority is effective under Probate Code § 4682. As to the form itself, the statute requires that a health care provider explain the POLST form and the medical interventions and procedures it offers, that the provider complete the form based on patient preferences and medical indications, and that the form be signed by a physician (or a nurse practitioner or physician assistant acting under the physician's supervision and within their scope of practice) and by Jordan Alex Lee or Jordan Alex Lee's legally recognized health care decisionmaker — here, Dr. Taylor Morgan, M.D. as the signing physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A legally recognized health care decisionmaker may execute the Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form only if the individual lacks capacity, or the individual has designated that the decisionmaker’s authority is effective pursuant to Section 4682."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(b) (California Legislative Information text), when a legally recognized health care decisionmaker may execute the form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4780.)
  "The Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form and medical intervention and procedures offered by the form shall be explained by a health care provider, as defined in Section 4621. The form shall be completed by a health care provider based on patient preferences and medical indications, and signed by a physician, or a nurse practitioner or a physician assistant acting under the supervision of the physician and within the scope of practice authorized by law, and the patient or his or her legally recognized health care decisionmaker."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(c) (California Legislative Information text), who must complete, explain, and sign the form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4780.)
  Known gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4780(b) and (c)), not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for these specific execution mechanics. The statute cross-references § 4682 (regarding when a decisionmaker's authority becomes effective) without this document independently verifying the text of § 4682 itself.

HOW A POLST FORM CAN BE REVOKED
An individual with capacity — Jordan Alex Lee, while having capacity — may revoke a POLST form at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke, consistent with Probate Code § 4695 (the same revocation standard the statute applies to most parts of an advance health care directive other than an agent designation).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An individual having capacity may revoke a Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke, consistent with Section 4695."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(d) (California Legislative Information text), revocation standard for a POLST form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4780.)
  Known gap: This clause rests on a single statutory subsection (§ 4780(d)); no additional independent source was located for this specific revocation rule for POLST forms. The statute cross-references § 4695 by number rather than restating its text within this Part; this document does not separately re-verify § 4695's text here (a companion Advance Health Care Directive document in this corpus verifies § 4695 directly). The statute does not, in this Part, address revocation by an individual who lacks capacity, or how a health care decisionmaker's own revocation authority for a POLST form is exercised once decisionmaker authority is in effect.

HEALTH CARE PROVIDERS COVERED, RELIANCE ON THE FORM, AND WHAT THE STATUTE DOES NOT SAY
The statute defines “health care provider” for purposes of this Part to include, without limitation, persons described in Probate Code § 4621 (health care professionals and institutions), as well as emergency response employees — including firefighters, law enforcement officers, EMT-I and EMT-II personnel, and paramedics — trained under Emergency Medical Services Authority standards. A health care provider who honors a request regarding resuscitative measures, including a POLST form, is not subject to criminal prosecution, civil liability, professional discipline, administrative sanction, or any other sanction as a result of that reliance, provided the provider believes in good faith the action is consistent with this Part and has no knowledge the action would be inconsistent with a decision the individual would have made personally. Separately, in the absence of knowledge to the contrary, a health care provider may presume a request regarding resuscitative measures — including a POLST form — is valid and unrevoked.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“health care provider” includes, but is not limited to, the following: (a) Persons described in Section 4621. (b) Emergency response employees, including, but not limited to, firefighters, law enforcement officers, emergency medical technicians I and II, paramedics, and employees and volunteer members of legally organized and recognized volunteer organizations, who are trained in accordance with standards adopted as regulations by the Emergency Medical Services Authority"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4781 (California Legislative Information text), definition of “health care provider” for this Part, including EMS/first-responder personnel (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4781.)
  "A health care provider who honors a request regarding resuscitative measures is not subject to criminal prosecution, civil liability, discipline for unprofessional conduct, administrative sanction, or any other sanction, as a result of his or her reliance on the request, if the health care provider (a) believes in good faith that the action or decision is consistent with this part, and (b) has no knowledge that the action or decision would be inconsistent with a health care decision that the individual signing the request would have made on his or her own behalf under like circumstances."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4782 (California Legislative Information text), immunity for a provider who honors the form in good faith (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4782.)
  "In the absence of knowledge to the contrary, a health care provider may presume that a request regarding resuscitative measures is valid and unrevoked."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4784 (California Legislative Information text), presumption of validity absent contrary knowledge (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4784.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on three independently numbered statutory sections (§§ 4781, 4782, and 4784), which are genuinely independent of one another rather than subsections of a single section. A notable gap: unlike the advance health care directive statute, this Part does not contain an explicit provision stating that a health care provider or EMS/first responder “must” honor a POLST form, nor does it state a rule for resolving a conflict between a POLST form and a later-expressed wish or a health care agent's decision. The statutory text instead (a) broadly defines who counts as a covered health care provider, (b) immunizes providers who honor the form in good faith, and (c) lets providers presume the form valid and unrevoked absent contrary knowledge — which functions as a practical incentive toward compliance without amounting to a codified duty to comply. Any rule about which document controls in a conflict is a matter of medical practice guidance outside the codified text reviewed here, and is not asserted as statutory law.

THIS PART DOES NOT DISPLACE OTHER HEALTH CARE DECISIONMAKING LAW
The Probate Code states that this Part on requests regarding resuscitative measures, including POLST forms, “does not repeal or narrow laws relating to health care decisionmaking.” It also states that the Part applies whether the individual executing a request regarding resuscitative measures is inside or outside a hospital or other health care institution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This part does not repeal or narrow laws relating to health care decisionmaking."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4786 (California Legislative Information text), this Part does not repeal or narrow other health care decisionmaking law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4786.)
  "This part applies regardless of whether the individual executing a request regarding resuscitative measures is within or outside a hospital or other health care institution."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4785 (California Legislative Information text), the Part applies regardless of location (in or outside a health care institution) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4785.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two independently numbered statutory sections (§§ 4785 and 4786) within the same Part; while both are part of Part 4 of Division 4.7, they are separately numbered, independently worded sections rather than subsections of one section. No portability or interstate-reciprocity provision was located anywhere in Probate Code §§ 4780–4786 for POLST forms; that topic is therefore omitted from this document rather than asserted without a verified citation.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT AND SIGNATURES
This document reflects Jordan Alex Lee's understanding, as of the date below, of the facts stated above regarding California's POLST framework under Probate Code §§ 4780–4786. It is not itself a completed Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form and creates no medical orders on its own. A POLST form, if completed, must separately be explained by a health care provider and signed by Jordan Alex Lee (or Jordan Alex Lee's legally recognized health care decisionmaker, Morgan Lee, if applicable under the statute described above) and by Dr. Taylor Morgan, M.D. as the supervising or signing physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant, on the EMSA-approved POLST form itself.

Patient / Decisionmaker Signature: ___________________________ Date: ______________

Print Name: Jordan Alex Lee

Physician / NP / PA Signature: ___________________________ Date: ______________

Print Name: Dr. Taylor Morgan, M.D.
